quests.instruction: In “Honestly, I’m running late”, how does “I’m” differ from “I am”?
options: “I’m” is one syllable, /aɪm/, while “I am” has two syllables
“I’m” drops the /m/, so it sounds like “eye”
“I’m” is the same as “I am”, only written shorter
“I’m” is stressed more strongly than “I am”
quests.correctAnswer: “I’m” is one syllable, /aɪm/, while “I am” has two syllables
quests.hint: Count the beats in “I’m” and in “I am”, saying each aloud quickly.
quests.explanation: A contraction is not just a shorter spelling: it is a different sound shape. “I’m” is a single syllable, /aɪm/, and “I am” is two, /aɪ æm/. Because the word is smaller, it sits easily in the rhythm of the sentence, and the /m/ attaches to the vowel. Recognising it helps you hear “I’m” as a short, quick sound.
quests.phoneticRule: A contraction merges a pronoun and an auxiliary into one syllable, so its pronunciation is shorter and differently shaped than the full two-word sequence.

quests.instruction: Why can “you’re” and “your” sound the same in “Aisha, you’re early today”?
options: “you’re” keeps two full syllables, /juː ɑː/, so the two words sound clearly different in fast speech
Both are unstressed and reduce to /jə/ or /jɔː/, so grammar and context tell them apart
“your” changes to the strong form /juː/ whenever an adjective follows it
“you’re” is silent in fast speech and only “early” is heard at all
quests.correctAnswer: Both are unstressed and reduce to /jə/ or /jɔː/, so grammar and context tell them apart
quests.hint: Say both words in a fast sentence and compare them. What do you notice about the vowel?
quests.explanation: In connected speech both “you’re” and “your” are weak and often sound like /jə/ or /jɔː/. Grammar, not sound, tells them apart: “you’re” is followed by an adjective or verb, “your” by a noun. So when you hear /jə/ plus “early”, you know it is “you’re early”.
quests.phoneticRule: Homophony between “you’re” and “your” is resolved by the following word class, not by pronunciation.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “we’ve” fits “Chloe, we’ve already eaten”?
options: “we have”: two full syllables, with a clear break
“wee”: the /v/ is dropped before the vowel
“weev”: one syllable, and its /v/ links onto “already”
“we-uv”: the /h/ is dropped but both syllables are kept
quests.correctAnswer: “weev”: one syllable, and its /v/ links onto “already”
quests.hint: Notice what follows “we’ve” and what the /v/ can do with it.
quests.explanation: “We’ve” is one syllable, /wiːv/, and “already” begins with a vowel, so the /v/ links onto it: “wee-vawl-ready”. The contraction therefore shortens the phrase and creates a link. If you listen only for “we have”, you may miss the sound.
quests.phoneticRule: Contracted “’ve” ends in /v/, which links onto a following vowel-initial word.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “don’t” fits “Dev, don’t forget the tickets”?
options: “don-tuh”: an extra vowel is added after the /t/, making two syllables
“dont”: said with a short /ɒ/ vowel, like the word “dot” with an /n/ added in the middle
“doan-t-forget”: the /t/ is pronounced twice, once for each word
“doan’”: one syllable with /əʊ/, and a weak or omitted /t/ before “forget”
quests.correctAnswer: “doan’”: one syllable with /əʊ/, and a weak or omitted /t/ before “forget”
quests.hint: Say “don’t forget” at a quick pace and decide how many syllables you really produce in “don’t”.
quests.explanation: “Don’t” is one syllable, /dəʊnt/. Before “forget” the final /t/ is in a crowded spot, so it is often weak or left out: “doan’ forget”. The vowel stays the same, which helps you tell it from “do”. Listening for the /əʊ/ vowel is more reliable than listening for the /t/.
quests.phoneticRule: Negative contractions keep their vowel but may lose or weaken the final /t/ before a consonant, so the vowel is the main cue.

quests.instruction: How many syllables does “wouldn’t” have in “Elena wouldn’t mind”?
options: Two: “wood-nt”, with a syllabic /n/ and no vowel before the /nt/
Three: “would-en-t”, with a full vowel before the /n/ and a clear final /t/
One: “woont”, with the /d/ lost
Two: “wood-ant”, with a clear /a/ vowel
quests.correctAnswer: Two: “wood-nt”, with a syllabic /n/ and no vowel before the /nt/
quests.hint: Say “wouldn’t” aloud and notice whether a vowel sounds between the /d/ and the /n/.
quests.explanation: “Wouldn’t” has two syllables: /ˈwʊdnt/. The second syllable is a syllabic /n/, with no vowel of its own. Learners who add a vowel (“would-en”) sound heavier than speakers who say /ˈwʊdnt/. The same happens in “didn’t”, “couldn’t” and “isn’t”.
quests.phoneticRule: Negative contractions with “-n’t” after a consonant form a syllabic /n/: the /n/ is the nucleus of the final syllable, with no vowel.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “won’t” fits “Farid won’t come tonight”?
options: /wɒnt/: the vowel is /ɒ/, like the word “want”, with a short vowel
/wʌnt/: the vowel is /ʌ/, like “won”
/wəʊnt/: the vowel is /əʊ/, like the vowel in “don’t”
/wɔːnt/: the vowel is /ɔː/, like “wart”
quests.correctAnswer: /wəʊnt/: the vowel is /əʊ/, like the vowel in “don’t”
quests.hint: Compare the vowel of “won’t” with the vowel of “don’t”, and then with the vowel of “want”.
quests.explanation: “Won’t” has the diphthong /əʊ/, so it rhymes with “don’t”. “Want” has the short vowel /ɒ/. The two words are easy to mix up, so the vowel is the key clue: “Farid woan’ come” means he will not come, while “Farid want come” would be ungrammatical.
quests.phoneticRule: “Won’t” has the diphthong /əʊ/, whereas “want” has /ɒ/, so the vowel separates two commonly confused words.

quests.instruction: Predict how “should’ve” is pronounced in “Grace should’ve called me”.
options: “should-have”: three syllables with a clear /h/ and a strong “have”
“shood-of”: a full /ɒv/ ending
“shood-əv”: two syllables, with a weak /əv/ and no /h/
“shood-ev”: a full /e/ vowel before the /v/
quests.correctAnswer: “shood-əv”: two syllables, with a weak /əv/ and no /h/
quests.hint: Say “should’ve” quickly and count the syllables. Which one is the weakest?
quests.explanation: “Should’ve” is two syllables: /ˈʃʊdəv/. The “’ve” is reduced to /əv/ with no /h/ and a weak vowel. This is why it can sound like “should of”, a common spelling mistake. In writing the correct form is “should have” or “should’ve”.
quests.phoneticRule: Because modal + ’ve ends in a weak /əv/, listeners cannot tell it from “of” by sound alone; the choice of “have” comes from grammar.

quests.instruction: Why does “must’ve” in “Hana must’ve forgotten” keep its /t/ before the weak “’ve”?
options: “must” is stressed, so it keeps every sound that is spelled
The /t/ is part of the spelling, so it must be pronounced in speech as well as in writing
The /v/ replaces the /t/ in fast speech
The weak /ə/ of “’ve” is a vowel, so the /t/ links onto it, not omitted
quests.correctAnswer: The weak /ə/ of “’ve” is a vowel, so the /t/ links onto it, not omitted
quests.hint: Recall what happens to a /t/ before a vowel and before a consonant.
quests.explanation: “Must’ve” is /ˈmʌstəv/. The /t/ is followed by the vowel of “’ve”, so it links onto it: “mus-təv”. Compare “must be”, where the /t/ is often omitted before a consonant. The same word can therefore behave differently depending on what follows.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final /t/ links before the vowel of a weak “’ve”, even in a cluster where it would otherwise be omitted before a consonant.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “might’ve” fits “Ivan might’ve missed it”?
options: “might-have”: two full words with a clear /h/ and a strong “have”
“my-əv”: the /t/ is dropped
“might-of”: a full /ɒv/ with stress on “of”, as in the spelling error
“my-təv”: the /t/ links onto the weak “’ve”, and there is no /h/
quests.correctAnswer: “my-təv”: the /t/ links onto the weak “’ve”, and there is no /h/
quests.hint: Predict what the /t/ of “might” does when a weak vowel follows.
quests.explanation: “Might’ve” is /ˈmaɪtəv/. The /t/ links onto the weak vowel of “’ve”, giving “my-təv”. There is no /h/ and no strong vowel. Looking for the /t/ plus a short schwa is the quickest way to recognise modal + ’ve in fast speech.
quests.phoneticRule: The /t/ of “might” links to the following weak /əv/, forming /ˈmaɪtəv/, with the same pattern as “must’ve”.

quests.instruction: In “Jade said she’d gone home”, does “she’d” mean “she would” or “she had”?
options: “She would”, because “said” is in the past
Either, because the sound shows which one
“She had”, because “gone” is a past participle
“She did”, because the /d/ stands for “did”
quests.correctAnswer: “She had”, because “gone” is a past participle
quests.hint: The sound of “’d” is the same for both, so look at the word that follows it.
quests.explanation: Both “would” and “had” contract to /d/, so the sound cannot decide. The next word does: a past participle (“gone”) means “had”, and a base verb means “would”. Here “gone” is a past participle, so “she’d” means “she had”. Listening for what follows is the key.
quests.phoneticRule: Contracted /d/ is ambiguous between “would” and “had”; the form of the following verb (past participle or base form) disambiguates it.

quests.instruction: In “Kofi, you’d better hurry”, what does “’d” stand for?
options: “Had”: “you’d better” means “you had better”
“Would”: it means “you would better”
“Did”: it means “you did better”
“Should”: it means “you should better”
quests.correctAnswer: “Had”: “you’d better” means “you had better”
quests.hint: Think about the fixed expression that ends in “better” and a base verb.
quests.explanation: “’d better” is a fixed expression that comes from “had better”, even though it is followed by a base verb (“hurry”). It does not mean “would”. So the usual rule (base verb means would) has an exception, and recognising “’d better” as a set phrase helps you avoid the trap.
quests.phoneticRule: “’d better” is an idiom derived from “had better”; it takes a base verb but is not “would”.

quests.instruction: Which meaning fits “he’d” in “Leo said he’d love to come”?
quests.word: Leo said he’d love to come
quests.textToSpeak: Leo said he’d love to come
options: “Had”, because “said” is in the past
“Would”, because “love” is a base verb
“Did”, because of “said”
“Could”, because “love” expresses ability
quests.correctAnswer: “Would”, because “love” is a base verb
quests.hint: Look at the form of the verb after “he’d”: base form or past participle?
quests.explanation: “Love” is a base form, not a past participle, so “he’d” is “he would”. “He’d love to come” is a polite way to say that he wants to come. Hearing the same /d/ in both uses, you must rely on grammar.
quests.phoneticRule: A base verb after contracted /d/ signals “would”; a past participle signals “had”.
quests.spokenForm: Leo sed heed love to come

quests.instruction: At work someone asks, “Who’ll be there on Monday?” Which spoken form of “who’ll” fits?
options: “who will”: two full syllables with a clear break
“who’d”: the /l/ becomes a /d/
“hool”: one syllable, with the /l/ joined to “who”
“whoa”: the /l/ is dropped completely
quests.correctAnswer: “hool”: one syllable, with the /l/ joined to “who”
quests.hint: Say “who’ll” alone, then in the question. How many syllables remain?
quests.explanation: “Who’ll” is one syllable, /huːl/. The /l/ closes the syllable, and it must not be dropped, or the word would become “who”. Question words are often contracted this way in workplace talk, so “who’ll” sounds like “hool”.
quests.phoneticRule: Question words contract with “’ll” as single syllables (who’ll, what’ll, where’ll), keeping a final /l/ that distinguishes them from the bare question word.

quests.instruction: How is “bus’ll” pronounced in “Tess says the bus’ll be late”?
quests.word: Tess says the bus’ll be late
quests.textToSpeak: Tess says the bus’ll be late
options: “bus-will”: the full word “will” with a strong vowel
“bus-ul”: two syllables, with a weak vowel before the /l/
“bus”: the “’ll” is silent
“bus-ill”: a stressed /ɪ/ vowel before the /l/
quests.correctAnswer: “bus-ul”: two syllables, with a weak vowel before the /l/
quests.hint: Contractions on nouns add a syllable. Listen for the small vowel before the /l/.
quests.explanation: A noun + “’ll” is pronounced with a weak vowel before the /l/: /ˈbʌsəl/, two syllables. The “’ll” is not silent and it is not a strong “will”. Spoken contractions on nouns are very common but rarely written in formal texts, so the pronunciation is a useful listening skill.
quests.phoneticRule: When “’ll” attaches to a noun ending in a consonant, a weak vowel /ə/ is inserted before /l/, giving /əl/ or a syllabic /l/.
quests.spokenForm: Tess says the buss-ul be late

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “there’s a” fits “Olga, there’s a problem”?
options: “there is a”: three full words with clear breaks
“there-sə”: the /z/ becomes /s/
“there-ə”: the /z/ is dropped
“there-zə”: the /z/ links onto the weak “a”
quests.correctAnswer: “there-zə”: the /z/ links onto the weak “a”
quests.hint: The contraction ends in /z/ and “a” is a weak vowel; decide what the two do together.
quests.explanation: “There’s” ends in /z/, and “a” is a weak vowel, so the /z/ links onto it: “there-zə”. The result sounds like one chunk, and a listener who expects “is” may not notice it. You hear this very often when someone announces a problem or a fact.
quests.phoneticRule: The /z/ of “’s” contractions links onto a following weak vowel-initial word, giving a chunk like /ðeəzə/.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “going to” is typical in “Paul, we’re going to leave soon”?
quests.word: Paul, we’re going to leave soon
quests.textToSpeak: Paul, we’re going to leave soon
options: “gonna”: /ˈɡɒnə/, with “going” shortened and “to” reduced to /ə/
“goh-ing too”: two full syllables for “going”, plus a strong “to”
“gonta”: the /t/ of “to” is kept and “going” loses its vowel
“gonner”: a noun, as in “a goner”, with a stressed second syllable
quests.correctAnswer: “gonna”: /ˈɡɒnə/, with “going” shortened and “to” reduced to /ə/
quests.hint: Say it as you would to a friend while grabbing your coat. How many syllables remain in “going to”?
quests.explanation: In casual speech “going to” is reduced to “gonna”: “going” loses its /ŋ/ and “to” becomes /ə/. It is an informal spoken form, common in conversation and in dialogue, but it is not used in formal writing. Recognising “gonna” is the first step; using it is optional.
quests.phoneticRule: “Gonna” is the informal spoken reduction of “going to” (future), with a weak /ə/ for “to”; it is not a standard written form.

quests.instruction: Which sound is lost when “want to” becomes “wanna” in “Rosa, do you want to eat now?”
quests.word: Rosa, do you want to eat now
quests.textToSpeak: Rosa, do you want to eat now
options: The /w/ at the start of “want”, so it sounds like “ant”
The /t/ of “want”, and “to” reduces to /ə/
The /n/ in the middle of “want”, leaving “wa-ta”
Nothing: “wanna” keeps both /t/ sounds
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ of “want”, and “to” reduces to /ə/
quests.hint: Compare “want to” and “wanna”, and find the consonant between the /n/ and the vowel that is missing.
quests.explanation: “Want to” becomes “wanna”: the /t/ of “want” is omitted (or merges), and “to” is reduced to a weak vowel /ə/, leaving /ˈwɒnə/. This is an informal spoken form and shows the same reduction pattern as “gonna”.
quests.phoneticRule: “Wanna” results from omission of the /t/ in “want” and reduction of “to” to /ə/, as an informal spoken form.
quests.spokenForm: Rosa, do you wanna eat now

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “got to” fits “Vera, we’ve got to go”?
options: “gonna”: the /t/ becomes an /n/ and the vowel stays
“goh-too”: two full syllables, with a long vowel in “to”
“gotta”: /ˈɡɒtə/, with the /t/ kept and “to” reduced to /ə/
“gotcha”: the /t/ blends with “to” into /tʃ/ and means “got you”
quests.correctAnswer: “gotta”: /ˈɡɒtə/, with the /t/ kept and “to” reduced to /ə/
quests.hint: In “got to”, the /t/ of “got” meets the weak “to”; think about what a /t/ can do before a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Got to” is reduced to “gotta”: the /t/ links onto the weak /ə/ of “to”, giving /ˈɡɒtə/. It is an informal spoken form, and it is not the same as “gotcha” (got you), which comes from a different blend. Recognising the three “-a” forms, gonna, wanna and gotta, is a good first step.
quests.phoneticRule: In “gotta” the /t/ of “got” links onto the weak vowel of “to”; the form is informal and conceptually similar to “gonna” and “wanna”.

quests.instruction: What happens to “kind of” in “Will, it’s kind of cold today”?
quests.word: Will, it’s kind of cold today
quests.textToSpeak: Will, it’s kind of cold today
options: “of” reduces to /ə/ and the /d/ links onto it: “kinda”
“kind” and “of” stay two full words with a clear break
“of” becomes “off”: “kind-off”
“kind” loses its /d/ and “of” loses its vowel: “kine-v”
quests.correctAnswer: “of” reduces to /ə/ and the /d/ links onto it: “kinda”
quests.hint: Say “kind of” as a hedge, quickly, before “cold”.
quests.explanation: “Kind of” is often used to soften a statement and is pronounced “kinda”: the /d/ links onto the weak /ə/ of “of”, and the /v/ is lost. It is informal. Hearing “kinda” helps you recognise a softened claim, as in “kind of cold”.
quests.phoneticRule: “Kinda” is the informal reduction of “kind of”, with /d/ linking to the weak /ə/ and loss of /v/.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “out of” fits “Tess ran out of time”?
options: “outta”: /ˈaʊtə/, with the /t/ linked to a weak “of”
“out-off”: a strong “off” after a pause
“out-uh-vuh”: two extra weak syllables
“ow-da”: the /t/ becomes a /d/
quests.correctAnswer: “outta”: /ˈaʊtə/, with the /t/ linked to a weak “of”
quests.hint: Say “ran out of time” quickly, the way someone panicking would.
quests.explanation: “Out of” becomes “outta”: the /t/ links onto the weak /ə/ of “of”, and the /v/ is lost: /ˈaʊtə/. It is an informal spoken form. You can hear it in “run outta time” and many similar phrases.
quests.phoneticRule: “Outta” is the informal reduction of “out of”, built on the same pattern as “kinda”: consonant links onto weak “of”, and /v/ is lost.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “sort of” fits “Uma was sort of angry”?
options: “sore-toff”: the /t/ links to a strong “off”
“sorter”: the word “sorter”, with a stressed second syllable
“sorta”: /ˈsɔːtə/, with the /t/ linked to a weak “of”
“saw-v”: the /t/ is lost
quests.correctAnswer: “sorta”: /ˈsɔːtə/, with the /t/ linked to a weak “of”
quests.hint: Predict the pattern from “kinda” and “outta” before you read the options.
quests.explanation: “Sort of” is reduced to “sorta”, just like “kind of” and “out of”: the final consonant links onto the weak /ə/ of “of”. It adds a hedge (“sort of angry” means “a little angry”). It is informal and spoken-only.
quests.phoneticRule: The “-a” reductions (kinda, sorta, outta, lotta) share one pattern: consonant + weak “of” becomes consonant + /ə/.

quests.instruction: On a call you hear “Honestly, I dunno.” Which standard phrase does “dunno” stand for?
options: “do know”: the “n’t” is dropped and the sentence becomes positive
“done know”: a different verb form
“don’t know”: /dəˈnəʊ/, with “don’t” weak and the /t/ lost
“didn’t know”: the past tense
quests.correctAnswer: “don’t know”: /dəˈnəʊ/, with “don’t” weak and the /t/ lost
quests.hint: Think about which negative words end in /nt/ and could lose their last sound before “know”.
quests.explanation: “Dunno” is the spoken form of “don’t know”: the vowel of “don’t” becomes weak, the /t/ is lost, and “know” keeps the /əʊ/ vowel: /dəˈnəʊ/. It is informal and spoken-only, and it is common in answers. Listening for the final /nəʊ/ helps you hear the negative.
quests.phoneticRule: “Dunno” is an informal contraction of “don’t know” in which “don’t” is reduced to /də/ and its /t/ is omitted.

quests.instruction: In a quick “Hana, lemme check”, which standard words does “lemme” stand for?
options: “let me”: the /t/ is lost and the words fuse
“left me”: a different verb with a stressed vowel
“let him”: a different pronoun with a dropped /h/
“lend me”: a different verb with a clear /n/ and /d/
quests.correctAnswer: “let me”: the /t/ is lost and the words fuse
quests.hint: Say “let me” very fast and notice what happens to the /t/.
quests.explanation: “Lemme” is the informal spoken form of “let me”: the /t/ assimilates to the /m/ or is lost, and the two syllables run together: /ˈlemi/. It is a spoken-only form that appears in casual speech and in informal dialogue. Recognising it shows how much the /t/ can vanish.
quests.phoneticRule: “Lemme” results from the /t/ of “let” assimilating or omitting before the /m/ of “me”, producing an informal fused form.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “give me” is typical in “Noah, give me a minute”?
options: “give-mee”: two full syllables with a clear /v/
“gimme”: /ˈɡɪmi/, with the /v/ merged into the /m/
“guy-mee”: a diphthong in the first syllable
“gime-ah-mi”: the vowels are all kept
quests.correctAnswer: “gimme”: /ˈɡɪmi/, with the /v/ merged into the /m/
quests.hint: Say “give me” fast, as if asking for time. Which sound is hardest to keep between the vowels?
quests.explanation: “Give me” becomes “gimme”: the /v/ merges into the /m/ (it assimilates), and the vowel shortens to /ɪ/: /ˈɡɪmi/. It is informal and it is spoken-only. Like “lemme” and “dunno”, it is worth recognising even if you do not use it.
quests.phoneticRule: In “gimme”, the /v/ assimilates to the following /m/ and the vowel shortens, producing an informal fused form of “give me”.

quests.instruction: In a job interview you want to say “Welcome everyone, I’m going to explain my plan.” Which delivery is the safest choice?
quests.word: Welcome everyone, I’m going to explain my plan
quests.textToSpeak: Welcome everyone, I’m going to explain my plan
options: “gonna”, because it sounds friendly and confident in an interview
“going to”, with natural linking and weak “to”, not “gonna”
“gonna”, with a fast and casual delivery to save time in the interview
“going to”, spoken very slowly with pauses
quests.correctAnswer: “going to”, with natural linking and weak “to”, not “gonna”
quests.hint: Think about audience and context: an interview where you want to be clear and professional.
quests.explanation: In a formal situation, the safest choice is the standard form, said at a natural pace: “going to”, with the weak /tə/ and linking, but without the casual “gonna”. You still use connected speech, just not the most informal forms. Choosing register is part of speaking well.
quests.phoneticRule: Register affects contraction choice: standard contractions and weak forms are acceptable in formal speech, while informal spoken-only forms such as “gonna” are better avoided.
quests.spokenForm: Welcome everyone, I’m goin’ tuh explain my plan

quests.instruction: Why should a formal email use “going to” and “want to” rather than “gonna” and “wanna”?
quests.word: Chloe is going to send the report
quests.textToSpeak: Chloe is going to send the report
options: “gonna” and “wanna” are grammatical mistakes in every context, whether spoken or written down
Spell-checkers cannot understand “gonna”, so the email would be rejected
The full forms are easier to pronounce, so they are used in writing
Informal spoken forms suit speech and casual messages; formal writing uses the full forms
quests.correctAnswer: Informal spoken forms suit speech and casual messages; formal writing uses the full forms
quests.hint: Ask who the reader is and what style they expect, compared with a chat between friends.
quests.explanation: “Gonna” and “wanna” represent speech. They appear in casual messages and in dialogue, but formal writing, such as reports and emails to clients, uses “going to” and “want to”. They are not mistakes; they are a different register. So the choice depends on audience, not on correctness.
quests.phoneticRule: Informal spoken forms are register-marked, not incorrect: they belong to casual speech and informal writing, while formal writing uses standard forms.

quests.instruction: In a client meeting you want to say “Frankly, we have to confirm the date.” Which spoken form is more suitable?
quests.word: Frankly, we have to confirm the date
quests.textToSpeak: Frankly, we have to confirm the date
options: “have to”, with natural weak forms (even “hafta”), not “gotta”
“gotta”, because it is shorter and saves time in the meeting
“gotcha”, because it sounds friendlier
“gonna have to”, because it sounds more confident to the client
quests.correctAnswer: “have to”, with natural weak forms (even “hafta”), not “gotta”
quests.hint: Think about which forms are informal markers, and which are ordinary connected speech.
quests.explanation: “Have to” with a weak /tə/ (and even the voicing change in “hafta”) is ordinary connected speech and suits a client meeting. “Gotta” is more clearly informal, so it is better kept for conversations with friends. You do not need to avoid all reductions, only the most informal ones.
quests.phoneticRule: Ordinary connected-speech reductions (weak forms, linking, standard contractions) are acceptable in professional speech; the informal -a forms are marked as casual.
quests.spokenForm: Frankly, we hafta confirm the date

quests.instruction: Which quick spoken form matches “Yara, I don’t know, we have got to ask”?
quests.word: Yara, I don’t know, we have got to ask
quests.textToSpeak: Yara, I don’t know, we have got to ask
options: “I dunno, we gonna ask”
“I donno, we wanna ask”
“I dun, we gotcha ask”
“I dunno, we gotta ask”
quests.correctAnswer: “I dunno, we gotta ask”
quests.hint: Match each reduction to its standard phrase: don’t know, have got to.
quests.explanation: “Don’t know” becomes “dunno”, and “got to” becomes “gotta”. The other options mix up the forms: “gonna” is for “going to”, “wanna” for “want to”, and “gotcha” for “got you”. Sorting the spoken-only forms by their standard sources is the skill this stage trains.
quests.phoneticRule: Each informal reduction maps to one standard source phrase: dunno (don’t know), gotta (got to), gonna (going to), wanna (want to).
quests.spokenForm: Yara, I dunno, we gotta ask

quests.instruction: Which quick spoken form matches “Kofi, we are going to run out of time”?
quests.word: Kofi, we are going to run out of time
quests.textToSpeak: Kofi, we are going to run out of time
options: “We’re gotta run outta time”
“We’re gonna run outta time”
“We’re wanna run outta time”
“We’re gonna run out time”
quests.correctAnswer: “We’re gonna run outta time”
quests.hint: Replace each standard phrase in turn: going to, out of.
quests.explanation: “Going to” becomes “gonna”, and “out of” becomes “outta”. “Gotta” and “wanna” would change the meaning, and dropping “of” altogether gives “run out time”, which is not a natural reduction. So the correct match keeps both reductions in their places.
quests.phoneticRule: A reduced form must keep the meaning of its source: gonna means going to and outta means out of; swapping them changes the sentence.
quests.spokenForm: Kofi, we’re gonna run outta time

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “is going to” is acceptable in speech but not in a formal report?
quests.word: Dana says the team is going to review it
quests.textToSpeak: Dana says the team is going to review it
options: “The team’s going to review it”
“The team is going to review it”
“The team’s about to review it”
“The team’s gonna review it”
quests.correctAnswer: “The team’s gonna review it”
quests.hint: Pick the option that contains a spoken-only form, not just a standard contraction.
quests.explanation: “The team’s” is a standard contraction and is fine in many written contexts. “Gonna” is the informal spoken form of “going to” and is better avoided in formal reports. So only the first option mixes a spoken-only reduction into the sentence.
quests.phoneticRule: Standard contractions (’s, ’ll, ’ve) are broadly acceptable, whereas informal spoken forms such as “gonna” should be kept for speech and casual writing.
quests.spokenForm: Dana says the team’s gonna review it
